{{Short description|Formula on random variables}}
[[File:Estimated and expected variance of cumulative sum.png|thumb|Estimated variance of the cumulative sum of iid normally distributed random variables (which could represent a [[gaussian random walk]] approximating a [[Wiener process]]). The sample variance is computed over 300 realizations of the corresponding random process.]]
In [[probability theory]], the general<ref>{{ cite book | last = Klenke | first = Achim | date = 2013 | title = Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie | page = 106 | url = https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-642-36018-3 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-642-36018-3}}</ref> form of '''Bienaymé's identity''', named for [[Irénée-Jules Bienaymé]], states that

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\operatorname{Var}\left( \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \right)
&= \sum_{i=1}^n \operatorname{Var}(X_i)+2\sum_{i,j=1 \atop i < j}^n \operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j) \\
&= \sum_{i,j=1}^n\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j).
\end{align}</math>

This can be simplified if <math>X_1, \ldots, X_n</math> are pairwise [[Independence (probability theory)|independent]] or just [[Uncorrelatedness (probability theory)|uncorrelated]], integrable [[random variable]]s, each with finite second [[Moment (mathematics)|moment]].<ref name="loeve" /> This simplification gives:

<math display="block">\operatorname{Var}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right) = \sum_{k=1}^n \operatorname{Var}(X_k).</math>

The above expression is sometimes referred to as Bienaymé's formula. Bienaymé's identity may be used in proving certain variants of the [[law of large numbers]].<ref name="ito" />
